I am pleased to present to the Preparatory Committee the final report of the Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems covering its work in 2024, 2025 and 2026. The Group adopted this report by consensus on Friday 4 September, concluding an intensive three-year period of work under the mandate given to us by the 2023 meeting of the High Contracting Parties. That mandate called upon the Group, in the context of the objectives and purpose of the Convention, to further consider and formulate by consensus a set of elements of an instrument without prejudging its nature and other possible measures to address emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems. To achieve this mandate, we were asked to build upon the Group's previous recommendations and conclusions, to take account of existing protocols within the Convention, proposals by the High Contracting Parties and other options concerning the normative and operational framework, and to bring together legal, military and technological expertise. Over the past three years, the Group devoted 30 days of formal meetings to this task. 10 days each in 2024, 2025, and 2026, divided into two sessions every year. This formal work was complemented by numerous informal consultations, which I convened throughout this three-year period. The process was demanding and often challenging. as delegations approached the issue from various perspectives and with different understandings of how the international community could and should respond to emerging technologies in the area of laws. Yet throughout our work, a shared commitment to engage with one another on substance remained, to build shared understandings and to seek areas of convergence where consensus may be achieved. To guide, structure, and advance the substantive exchanges, the Group worked on the basis of a rolling text, suggested by me as Chair during its second session in 2024. This rolling text contained a draft set of elements of an instrument and other possible measures, as per the mandate of the GGE. These were formed as a synthesis of proposals and positions brought forward by States during the first session. The intersessional period and previous work of the GDE. The text guided the group's work over two and a half years and became an essential tool through which delegations were able to engage in detailed technical exchanges that served to move from political positioning to legal, military and technological consideration. From its first iteration in 2024 to its finalization last week, the text, and with it our understanding, has come a long way. Mr. Chair, the set of elements and other possible measures initially contained in this rolling text became the principal substantive outcome of the work of the Group, and the elements are contained in the conclusions of the report in their final iteration. This is a monumental result. The agreed elements address a broad range of issues that have occupied the Group since its inception. This includes a characterization of lethal autonomous weapons systems within the framework of the CCW. That not only ensures a common understanding of what we are addressing, but also seeks to withstand the test of time in order to render it useful for years to come. an affirmation of the applicability of international humanitarian law relating to laws and related prohibitions, regulations, and specifications, a requirement of controlling human judgment to ensure compliance with international law applicable in armed conflict, including a specification of how such control and human judgment is exercised and relevant measures in this regard. A broad range of risk mitigation measures relevant at various stages of the life cycle of a law that are underpinned by a requirement that the use and anticipated effects of laws in different circumstances can be understood. And last and finally, as well as measures related to responsibility and accountability. Taken together, the set of elements and other possible measures represent the product of sustained negotiation and compromise among High Contracting Parties. Their significance lies not only in each individual paragraph, but also in the fact that the Group was able to formulate them by consensus under the mandate entrusted to it. Mr. Chair, allow me to say a few words about the process that brought us here. From the beginning, I sought to conduct the work of the Group in a transparent and inclusive manner, progressively focusing our discussions on areas that might command consensus, but never shying away from those that were less likely to do so. The considerable number of working papers and textual suggestions submitted by High Contracting Parties, observers, as well as by me as the Chair, provided important contribution to that effort. We want to highlight two particular advances made by the GGE. First, the group reached consensus on a characterization of lethal autonomous weapons systems. This has long eluded us, in part because of the rapidly advancing technologies that underpin these systems. and the need to ensure that we were not being overly or underly inclusive to achieve consensus. The characterization describes in a flexible and clear way what about laws is distinctive as compared to other types of weapons. The group also made tremendous progress in elaborating the human element. In particular, the paragraphs explaining the concepts of control and human judgment in the context of compliance with IHL and the use of lethal autonomous weapon systems reflects critical advances in our collective thinking. Delegations came at these issues from many different perspectives, but the group took the time to come to consensus and explain the necessity for control and human judgment in upholding compliance with IHL, as well as how those concepts relate to each other and to the measures that can support IHL compliance. Even while taking stock of these tremendous accomplishments, I think we all acknowledge that there is still much work to do. Last week helped us identify issues on which the group simply needs more time to make more progress. These include, for example, a further elaboration of how existing IHL rules apply to the use of these weapons systems, as well as when and how modifications of the systems should be reviewed. The group did not have enough time to gain consensus on these topics and others, but their further exploration is key to continued work on lethal autonomous weapons systems in the CCW process. We hope that the work is continued under a future LOS mandate and that it will provide the group time to make further progress on these and other issues. Let us build on this momentum and the expert-driven process by further elaborating and clarifying how IHL rules apply to the use of laws, and what specific measures states should implement to support compliance with their IHL obligations. Regardless of the words of a future mandate, it is clear that we will need the resources and modalities necessary to complete the task. This includes sufficient time and almost certainly a multi-year mandate with more annual sessions for the work needed to formulate the mandated outcome. To develop an instrument, work on legal and technical issues would be needed in even more detail than in the past. It therefore is necessary to consider new modalities to facilitate that work, such as subgroups within the mandated body that are devoted to specific legal or technical issues. Perhaps just as importantly, the group will need to stay current on matters that are the subject of rapid developments in technology and state practice. To that end, voluntary exchanges among states on their practice on implementing their IHL obligations in the context of lethal autonomous weapon systems would directly inform the elaboration of an instrument and also serve as a confidence building and transparency measure that will be beneficial on its own. Clearly, there is a range of views on how best to take the success of the GGE forward. Whatever path we choose, we should prioritize advancement of substantive dialogue within the CCW framework, which has just shown that it can deliver. Thank you for your time.

Second, the review conference should take a decision to establish a negotiation mandate for an instrument on autonomous weapons systems. It is high time we moved from discussions to concrete regulations. With a negotiations mandate and a defined goal and instrument, we will enable ourselves to change gears and make effective progress within a forum that is uniquely well suited to tackle this complex, multidisciplinary issue. The discussions on laws date back more than a decade. After 10 years of discussing legal, technical, ethical and military aspects of laws, as well as operational and other frameworks on laws, the CCW in 2023 gave the GGE a mandate to formulate a set of elements for an instrument on laws, not just elements on laws in general, but elements of an instrument specifically. That set of elements has now been concluded. The elements formulated by the DG have clear shortcomings, in our view. They only list some measures relevant to maintaining human control over laws, and a number of important measures did not reach sufficient maturity in time and were therefore not carried forward into the final text. That includes, for example, requirements relating to human authorisation of material modifications to mission and target parameters. Similarly, the importance of ensuring that laws remain reliable, predictable and adequately explainable and traceable was not ultimately reflected in the report. The task of determining where the limits of acceptable autonomy lie remains ahead of us. Yet the elements also represent substantial progress, showing the continued relevance and considerable value of the CCW. Working characterization for laws was finally achieved. The need for control and human judgment to ensure compliance with IHL was recognized. A number of basic measures to ensure that humans retain such control were laid out. And the need for bias mitigation was highlighted, and a range of other measures to reduce risks and promote human responsibility and accountability were set out. Taken together, the elements provide the necessary basis, and a sufficient basis at that, for negotiations on the actual instrument to commence. Although many issues discussed did not make it into the GGE final report, the very rich discussions for more than a decade now provide an important body of work on which further progress can be built. As underscored in a number of joint statements over the past year, the various outstanding issues can and should be resolved in the negotiations on the instrument itself. We just needed a starting point, and now we have one, one that neither prejudices the scope, outcome, or nature of that instrument. The negotiations can and likely should be supplemented with meetings of specific substance matter experts as necessary, like the negotiation mandates on explosive remnants of war in the early 2000s provided for. Finally, on the issue of the nature of the instrument, we believe that the mandate should open for a combination of prohibitions, regulations and guidelines, as well as other understandings. Although a legally binding instrument should, in our opinion, be an aim of those negotiations, the mandate should not exclude the development of other practical measures and guidelines that, in our view, also have an important role to play. We are ready to work with all delegations in pursuit of a successful and meaningful outcome at the seventh review conference.

Questions related to the use of explosive weapons and relevant problems is directly related with the question of strict compliance of existing provisions of international legal instruments. For example, the Additional Protocol I of 1977 to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. as well as the CCW and its protocols. We believe that existing legal regulations to be sufficient. Moreover, we have serious doubts that the question of the use of explosive weapons actually falls within the mandate of the convention. Rather, this is an issue that should be discussed in four that discusses issues related to the implementation of IHL, we do not see any need to develop any new norms or carry out separate expert-based work within the CCW in connection with the question of EWIPA. We also cannot support separate initiatives to introduce for discussions here in the CCW of additional issues that we believe have little connection to the Convention, for example, the issue of gender. We believe that such issues do not have any direct connection to the objectives and purposes of the Convention, and we do not find it advisable to introduce these questions for any separate discussions during the upcoming Seventh Review Conference. Thank you.

Thank you, Russia, for your precisions. And I now begin with my list of speakers of the observers to this process. May I give the floor to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the ICRC. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. And the ICRC joins others in congratulating you on your appointment as Chair of the Main Committee, too. Mr. Chair, we would like to commend the Group of Governmental Experts on Laws for reaching consensus and successfully completing its mandate in a difficult environment. We particularly note the outstanding work done by the Chair, Ambassador Indenbosch, and his team, along with the CCW ISU, for creating the conditions that facilitated this consensus. We were encouraged by the large number of States that showed a clear willingness to finalise the mandate and progress towards negotiations. And we welcome the joint statements last week made by Brazil on behalf of 47 states and by Algeria on behalf of the African group in this regard. Mr. Chair, the group made significant progress over its three years. It developed a substantial corpus of work, including a working characterization of lethal autonomous weapons systems and a structure of prohibitions and restrictions. Importantly, the final report affirmed that control and human judgment must be retained in the use of force, and that accountability for decisions involving the use of autonomous weapons cannot be transferred to a machine. This aligns with what the ICRC has emphasized for many years, and its inclusion in the report is significant. The report does not take the next step of translating these findings into the specific operational guidance that is needed to give direction to those developing and using these weapons. It rather recalls general principles and rules of IHL. This is a missed opportunity, but it is far from a dead end. Taken together, the final report and the substantial body of work developed by the group, by the chair, and by states over the past three years constitute a strong and sufficient basis to launch negotiations on a legally binding instrument. Outstanding issues, including a prohibition on anti-personnel autonomous weapon systems, and a prohibition on unpredictable autonomous weapons systems, which found broad support throughout the Group's mandate but was not retained in the final text, can and should be resolved within those negotiations and not used as a reason to delay them further. Mr. Chair, we would like to highlight once again that the Group has completed its mandate. It is finished, concluded, finalised and done. It is achieved, accomplished, realized, and affected. It is fulfilled, consummated, executed, and discharged. In short, Mr. Chair, it is an X mandate. The group has formulated a set of elements of an instrument to address emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems. The next step, and really the only step that makes sense, is obviously to create the instrument that will contain these elements. The ICRC therefore reiterates its call on States to take the decision at the November Review Conference to launch negotiations on a new protocol to the CCW on autonomous weapons systems. In line with our role under the CCW's rules of procedure and our mandate to promote and strengthen respect for international humanitarian law, the ICRC stands ready to support States with our legal and policy expertise throughout this process. We continue to stress the urgency of this exercise. To delay further is not an option. Thank you.
Thank you very much to the ICRC representative. I now give the floor to Matt for Peace. Matt for Peace, you have the floor.

We wish to welcome the consensus made in Geneva after the meeting of the GGE on autonomous weapons and the affirmation that human control should not be transferred to machines. However, this is not enough to address the challenges and the rapid movement into Integrating artificial intelligence in the battlefield. In this regard, NATO expresses its concern regarding the omission of crucial elements from the agreed-upon text. We call for the explicit inclusion, most importantly, reliability and predictability of behavior as a prerequisite for any development or deployment, full traceability of algorithmic decisions, strict safeguards preventing the modification of objectives without direct human authorization, a commitment to conducting periodic legal reviews of systems after any technical modification. Regarding human control, MAD insists that weapon systems must be subject to effective human control and oversight throughout their life cycle, including design, testing, deployment, and use. Human intervention must retain the ability to intervene immediately and disable systems. Precise operational constraints must be established, encompassing timeframes, geographic scope, and target type. Matt, emphasizes the need for a two-pronged approach that combines prohibiting systems that pose unacceptable risks with regulating other military applications of artificial intelligence. We stress in this respect, Mr. Chair, that the prohibition must include the systems that lack transparency or whose behavior, effects, and control cannot be adequately understood or controlled. In conclusion, Mr. President, we call for a balanced approach to make the best use of AI while transferring the technology, transferring the technology for developing countries in order to prevent any monopoly over them. Thank you.
Shukran kithir to MAAD for Peace. I now give the floor to the International Humanitarian Law Youth Initiative, the IHL-YI. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. We congratulate you on the chairmanship of the Main Committee II. The IHL-YI welcomes the presentation of the final report of the Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems. We would also like to express our appreciation to the GGE Chair and his team and the CCW ISU for their efforts throughout this process. For us, this is also an especially meaningful moment. We have been engaged in the discussions on autonomous weapons for several years. and over the past three years, through IHOYI, we have worked with a great commitment to contribute to the discussions and negotiations, raise awareness and bring the perspectives of young lawyers, academics, researchers and civil society into this process. We welcome the consensus reached on the final report. In the current international context, achieving consensus among states is an important accomplishment. We also welcome the reaffirmation of the applicability of international law, including international humanitarian law, the importance of human judgment and control, and the principle that human responsibility and accountability cannot be transferred to machines. However, we believe that consensus should be understood as a starting point, not the end of the discussion. In this regard, we would like to offer the following recommendations for the way forward. First, States should build upon the elements developed through the work of the GGE and ensure that consensus does not result in weakening or rolling back important elements developed over the past three years. Second, States should continue working towards clear prohibitions and restrictions on autonomous weapons systems or their use where compliance with international humanitarian law cannot be ensured or where they present unacceptable humanitarian, legal, or ethical risks. Third, Issues of reliability, predictability, traceability, testing, and legal review should be addressed through the life cycle of autonomous weapon systems, including following significant modifications to these systems. Fourth, discussions should move beyond reaffirming general principles towards clearer and more effective rules and mechanisms to ensure human responsibility, meaningful human judgment and effective human control over the use of force. Fifth, States should use the seventh review conference in November as an opportunity to move from years of discussion towards concrete steps for the development of a legally binding international framework to regulate autonomous weapons. We also emphasize the importance of continued meaningful and sustained participation of young people and civil society in the next phase of this process. Young people should not be simply recipients of these discussions, but active contributors to shaping the rules that will govern the future of warfare and technology. The GGE has concluded its mandate, but the responsibility to address the humanitarian, legal, and ethical challenges posed by autonomous weapons remains. Consensus is important, but it should be the beginning of more ambitious action, not the ceiling of what states can achieve. I thank you.
